title: Year three close: the great story
hookLine: the whole story from the palace to today

lines: HAND TO HAND, ROAD TO ROAD.
cards: A gate opens at night, and a prince rides out of his father's palace. In the poem that opened this year, that night is the turning point of the great story. It doesn't end there, and it doesn't end with him.
It runs on, hand to hand, road to road, to a temple down some street near you, a lamp on a windowsill, a person sitting still for two minutes on an ordinary morning.
Today, the last day of year three: the whole story, from that gate to today.

teach.h: THE PALACE, THE TREE, THE DEER PARK.
teach.b: The prince sees age, sickness and death, and a wanderer at peace, and he leaves. He strives until he is thin as a shadow.
He sits beneath a tree; Mara comes with his army of desire and doubt, and the seeker doesn't get up. He wakes up. At the deer park he turns the wheel of the teaching for his old companions.
Friends come, then strangers, then kings and courtesans and outcasts. Women ask to be ordained, and an order of nuns begins.

For years he walks the roads and teaches, and at the end, lying between two trees, he gives his last instruction, the one you heard on the day of renewal: in paraphrase, all made things come apart, so keep going with care.
Then the story passes to other hands. The elders meet and recite what they remember.

Reciters carry it by memory; later, tradition says, scribes write it down. An emperor carves teachings into stone. Monks and nuns carry it south across the sea and north along the caravan roads, into new languages.
Teachers argue, explain, and build new schools on it. Buddhists tell some parts differently: which texts come first, which teachers matter most. Each school keeps its own telling.
Then the hard chapters: monasteries burned, monks killed, texts lost.
And each time, someone gathers what's left and begins again. Which brings the story here: to temples far from where it started, to chaplains in hospitals, to festivals with sweet tea and lamps.
A story that started with one person leaving home is now kept by people in many homes.

how: Buddhists tell the Buddha's life and the story of the teaching at festivals, in temple paintings and in chanting, and some communities close a year of study by dedicating its merit to others.

o: a god who rules over the heavens
the awakened one, a title, not a name
the prince's family name from birth

games.q: you know the story now: tap the pairs.
p: the wheel of the teaching first turned

s: the story ends with the Buddha's death
it passes to the elders, the reciters, the roads, the teachers, and on to today.
Buddhists tell some parts of the story differently
which texts come first and which teachers matter most; each school keeps its own telling.
the story stayed in one land and one language
monks and nuns carried it south across the sea and north along the caravan roads, into new languages.

games.q: you've heard the whole story, from the palace gate to today. the year is over. what does the path ask of you now?
games.why: the last day of the year asks only for rest and a long look out, the way the story itself went out through the gate.

practice: If there's a window near you, turn toward it; if not, a doorway, or the far side of the room.
Let your eyes rest there without naming anything, and let your attention go out the way the story went through the palace gate, gently, then back to the breath. Nothing to finish; just rest.

wordCard.voice: Buddha. The awakened one at the center of the great story, from the palace gate to the people keeping it today, and the end of the third year on this path. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: the title of the one at the center of the story, usually given in English as the awakened one.

carryVoice: Your line: you know the story now. Tomorrow, year four opens with the higher teaching. Year three, complete.
